I liked that book. What didn't you like about it?

I'll admit, as political commentary the ultimate game concept is a little facile, but the book also raised, for me, interesting questions regarding foreign policy and whether it's moral to meddle or try to control other cultures.

First, there was no epic conflict. Gurgeh might have his name tarnished? Oh no! That just seemed like a very weak plot device.

Second, without a great conflict, there can be no satisfying resolution. No revenge was had. It was more like the story just progressed forward one more step.

Gurgeh felt very one dimensional. I never could read his personality. The robots seemed more lively to me.

I was expecting there to be some grand complicate problem in a game with some elegant solution revealed at the end, and the book never had such a prize. The emotions of the games were discussed, but never the heart of the mechanics.

Interesting. I interpreted his motivation and the main plot conflict to be the puzzle and challenge of mastering a new game with secondary plot motivation being his inner conflict between his desire for the challenge and his suspicition that he was being manipulated.

While the ending didn't wrap everything up nicely, I thought it had a great feeling of ambiguity whether Gurgeh was playing the part of a pawn in an even larger and more complex game and whether the faction in that game that he played for was acting morally.

There were parts I like. The politics were interesting. The idea of Gurgeh being played as a game within the game was interesting. Everything just felt very flat to me. The grand reveal ( was just very anti-climatic. The best thing I like about it was how cool the culture was, but all that was secondary to the main plot of Gurgeh playing a board game in which I'm still a little puzzled over what he really won.

So, I'm open to another Ian Banks, but Player of Games didn't do it for me.
